We propose using sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to create SAE embeddings: representations whose dimensions map to interpretable concepts. Through four data analysis tasks, we show that SAE embeddings are more cost-effective and reliable than LLMs and more controllable than dense embeddings. Using the large hypothesis space of SAEs, we can uncover insights such as (1) semantic differences between datasets and (2) unexpected concept correlations in documents. For instance, by comparing model responses, we find that Grok-4 clarifies ambiguities more often than nine other frontier models. Relative to LLMs, SAE embeddings uncover bigger differences at 2-8x lower cost and identify biases more reliably. Additionally, SAE embeddings are controllable: by filtering concepts, we can (3) cluster documents along axes of interest and (4) outperform dense embeddings on property-based retrieval. Using SAE embeddings, we study model behavior with two case studies: investigating how OpenAI model behavior has changed over time and finding "trigger" phrases learned by Tulu-3 (Lambert et al., 2024) from its training data. These results position SAEs as a versatile tool for unstructured data analysis and highlight the neglected importance of interpreting models through their data.

papers.title: SAEBench: A Comprehensive Benchmark for Sparse Autoencoders in Language Model Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate dictionary learning (sparse autoencoders) for language model interpretability beyond unsupervised proxy metrics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAEBench, a comprehensive benchmark with eight metrics to evaluate sparse autoencoders for language model interpretability, and provides an open-source suite of over 200 SAEs for systematic comparison.
papers.conclusion: SAEBench provides a standardized framework for evaluating SAEs, revealing that proxy metrics are insufficient and that different architectures excel at different aspects of interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Gains on proxy metrics (sparsity-fidelity) do not reliably translate to better practical performance.
Matryoshka SAEs perform well on feature disentanglement metrics despite underperforming on proxy metrics.
Scaling SAE width has mixed effects: some metrics improve, but feature disentanglement metrics often degrade except for Matryoshka SAEs.
No single sparsity level is optimal for all tasks; moderate sparsity (L0 50-150) offers a reasonable compromise.
ReLU SAEs are outperformed by newer architectures on most metrics.
papers.limitation: The metrics were designed for evaluating SAEs on the same underlying model, not for comparing SAEs across fundamentally different models such as fully trained versus randomly initialized.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular technique for interpreting language model activations, and there is extensive recent work on improving SAE effectiveness. However, most prior work evaluates progress using unsupervised proxy metrics with unclear practical relevance. We introduce SAEBench, a comprehensive evaluation suite that measures SAE performance across eight diverse metrics, spanning interpretability, feature disentanglement and practical applications like unlearning. To enable systematic comparison, we open-source a suite of over 200 SAEs across eight recently proposed SAE architectures and training algorithms. Our evaluation reveals that gains on proxy metrics do not reliably translate to better practical performance. For instance, while Matryoshka SAEs slightly underperform on existing proxy metrics, they substantially outperform other architectures on feature disentanglement metrics; moreover, this advantage grows with SAE scale. By providing a standardized framework for measuring progress in SAE development, SAEBench enables researchers to study scaling trends and make nuanced comparisons between different SAE architectures and training methodologies. Our interactive interface enables researchers to flexibly visualize relationships between metrics across hundreds of open-source SAEs at: www.neuronpedia.org/sae-bench

papers.title: Don't Forget It! Conditional Sparse Autoencoder Clamping Works for Unlearning
papers.research_question: How can Sparse Autoencoders be used to unlearn harmful knowledge in large language models while retaining safe knowledge?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a conditional SAE-based clamping method for unlearning that improves retention of safe information compared to prior SAE methods and performs comparably to RMU with better interpretability.
papers.conclusion: SAE-based unlearning outperforms prior SAE approaches on retention and performs comparably with RMU on forgetting harmful information while retaining safe information, with fewer hyperparameters and better interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Refusal Clamp achieves the lowest WMDP-bio accuracy (0.2718) and highest alignment score (0.8226), indicating effective unlearning with some impact on general knowledge.
Clamp Prime improves forgetting performance (WMDP-bio accuracy drops to 0.2985) but slightly reduces general knowledge retention compared to RMU.
Adversarial evaluation using Concurrent Greedy Search shows that unlearned models resist suffix attacks, continuing to output gibberish.
The method requires fewer hyperparameter choices than RMU while maintaining interpretability.
SAE-based unlearning is shown to be viable, with conditional steering reducing side effects on safe information.
papers.limitation:
Training sparse autoencoders and labeling the latents is slow and expensive, limiting practicality to models with pre-existing SAEs.
Steering models with sparse autoencoders requires closed weights, as attackers can remove steering hooks if they have access to the weights.
Using Wikitext as the retain set for RMU may cause bias, potentially inflating the method's score on biology-related subjects in evaluation.
future_direction: Investigating which SAE layers allow for the best unlearning.
Exploring the impact of latent space dimensionality (i.e., using SAEs with larger hidden activation shapes).
Training interpretable parameters that edit the SAE latent vector to allow for fully interpretable fine-tuning.
papers.abstract: Recent developments in Large Language Model (LLM) capabilities have brought great potential but also posed new risks. For example, LLMs with knowledge of bioweapons, advanced chemistry, or cyberattacks could cause violence if placed in the wrong hands or during malfunctions. Because of their nature as near-black boxes, intuitive interpretation of LLM internals remains an open research question, preventing developers from easily controlling model behavior and capabilities. The use of Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) has recently emerged as a potential method of unraveling representations of concepts in LLMs internals, and has allowed developers to steer model outputs by directly modifying the hidden activations. In this paper, we use SAEs to identify unwanted concepts from the Weapons of Mass Destruction Proxy (WMDP) dataset within gemma-2-2b internals and use feature steering to reduce the model's ability to answer harmful questions while retaining its performance on harmless queries. Our results bring back optimism to the viability of SAE-based explicit knowledge unlearning techniques.

papers.title: Evaluating Sparse Autoencoders for Monosemantic Representation
papers.research_question: How do concept activation distributions differ between Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and their base models, and do SAEs promote more monosemantic representations?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a distribution-aware concept separability score and shows that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability than their dense base models. It also proposes a new intervention method, Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), which enables effective concept removal with minimal side effects.
papers.conclusion: This work presents the first quantitative analysis of monosemanticity in SAEs compared to dense base models through a distributional lens, introduces a fine-grained concept separability score, and proposes a new intervention method (APP) that achieves effective concept removal with the least possible side effects.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs exhibit lower polysemanticity (neuron overlap) and higher concept separability than their base models across multiple datasets and models.
SAEs enable more precise concept-level interventions than base models, particularly when using partial suppression methods.
The proposed APP intervention method achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly competitive at concept removal.
Higher-capacity SAEs (e.g., 65k dimensions) yield greater concept separability and more effective interventions than lower-capacity ones.
A strong positive correlation exists between the concept separability score and the precision of partial concept erasure methods.
papers.limitation: APP uses a histogram-based approximation for density estimation to improve computational efficiency, which trades off accuracy and computational cost. Achieving the best possible performance requires significantly higher computational resources.
future_direction: Future work could explore alternative kernel density estimation (KDE) methods to better balance accuracy and efficiency for the APP method.
papers.abstract: A key barrier to interpreting large language models is polysemanticity, where neurons activate for multiple unrelated concepts. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have been proposed to mitigate this issue by transforming dense activations into sparse, more interpretable features. While prior work suggests that SAEs promote monosemanticity, no quantitative comparison has examined how concept activation distributions differ between SAEs and their base models. This paper provides the first systematic evaluation of SAEs against base models through activation distribution lens. We introduce a fine-grained concept separability score based on the Jensen-Shannon distance, which captures how distinctly a neuron's activation distributions vary across concepts. Using two large language models (Gemma-2-2B and DeepSeek-R1) and multiple SAE variants across five datasets (including word-level and sentence-level), we show that SAEs reduce polysemanticity and achieve higher concept separability. To assess practical utility, we evaluate concept-level interventions using two strategies: full neuron masking and partial suppression. We find that, compared to base models, SAEs enable more precise concept-level control when using partial suppression. Building on this, we propose Attenuation via Posterior Probabilities (APP), a new intervention method that uses concept-conditioned activation distributions for targeted suppression. APP achieves the smallest perplexity increase while remaining highly effective at concept removal.

papers.title: Mechanistic Permutability: Match Features Across Layers
papers.research_question: How do interpretable features extracted by Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) evolve across layers in neural networks, and how can we align these features across layers without using input data?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Match, a data-free method for aligning Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across neural network layers, and parameter folding, a technique that incorporates activation thresholds into SAE weights to account for feature scale differences and improve matching.
papers.conclusion: SAE Match advances mechanistic interpretability by providing a data-free tool for analyzing feature dynamics across layers, validated on Gemma 2, showing effective feature matching and persistence, and enabling approximation of hidden states.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Match effectively captures feature evolution across layers, improving feature matching quality.
Features persist over several layers, with similarity gradually declining but remaining significant for approximately five layers.
The method can approximate hidden states across layers, enabling layer pruning with minimal performance loss from the 10th layer onward.
Parameter folding, which incorporates activation thresholds into SAE weights, improves matching quality by accounting for differences in feature scales.
Matching quality is lower in initial layers (before layer 10), possibly due to more polysemantic features and differences in SAE sparsity (l0 norms).
papers.limitation:
The current work uses a scheme matching all SAE weights (encoder, decoder, biases); future studies may need a more precise understanding of the behavior of different weights within the module.
The method uses bijective matching, but some features are not matched in this way, suggesting a need for more sophisticated methods to understand feature dynamics.
Selecting appropriate SAEs based on their l0 value (sparsity) is important, as differences in l0 norms between layers can affect matching performance, especially in early layers.
future_direction: More precise understanding of the behavior of different SAE weights (encoder, decoder, biases) in matching.
Selecting SAEs based on their l0 value (sparsity) to improve matching, especially in early layers.
Exploring more sophisticated, non-bijective methods to understand feature dynamics when features are not perfectly matched.
papers.abstract: Understanding how features evolve across layers in deep neural networks is a fundamental challenge in mechanistic interpretability, particularly due to polysemanticity and feature superposition. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have been used to extract interpretable features from individual layers, aligning these features across layers has remained an open problem. In this paper, we introduce SAE Match, a novel, data-free method for aligning SAE features across different layers of a neural network. Our approach involves matching features by minimizing the mean squared error between the folded parameters of SAEs, a technique that incorporates activation thresholds into the encoder and decoder weights to account for differences in feature scales. Through extensive experiments on the Gemma 2 language model, we demonstrate that our method effectively captures feature evolution across layers, improving feature matching quality. We also show that features persist over several layers and that our approach can approximate hidden states across layers. Our work advances the understanding of feature dynamics in neural networks and provides a new tool for mechanistic interpretability studies.

papers.title: Emergence of Biological Structural Discovery in General-Purpose Language Models
papers.research_question: Can general-purpose language models infer biological structural logic through abstract reasoning without domain-specific training, or is it dependent on massive biological data?
papers.core_contribution: General-purpose language models possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery through cross-modal transfer from linguistic syntax, enabling zero-shot performance on tasks like protein homology detection without domain-specific training.
papers.conclusion: The deep isomorphism between human language and biological sequences suggests that syntax is a universal property of organized information, and general-purpose LLMs can serve as powerful probes for decoding biological structure without domain-specific training.
papers.key_findings:
A GPT-2 model fine-tuned on English paraphrasing achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, demonstrating cross-modal syntactic transfer.
Scaling to large models like Qwen-3 reveals a phase transition to near-perfect accuracy on standard tasks and maintains 75% precision on remote homology datasets.
Chain-of-Thought analysis shows that models perform 'mental folding', leveraging implicit structural knowledge for reasoning beyond sequence alignment.
The capability extends to DNA homology and Central Dogma mapping, with performance varying based on model scale and pre-training exposure.
The BioPAWS benchmark is introduced to standardize evaluation of cross-modal biological understanding in LLMs.
papers.limitation: Generative tasks such as de novo design of functional enzymes may lead to biologically plausible but physically unstable structures due to hallucinations.
future_direction: Hybrid architecture using general LLMs as high-level architects and domain-specific models as engineers to enforce physical constraints.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Large language models (LLMs) are evolving into engines for scientific discovery, yet the assumption that biological understanding requires domain-specific pre-training remains unchallenged. Here, we report that general-purpose LLMs possess an emergent capability for biological structural discovery. First, we demonstrate that a small-scale GPT-2, fine-tuned solely on English paraphrasing, achieves ~84% zero-shot accuracy in protein homology detection, where network-based interpretability confirms a deep structural isomorphism between human language and the language of life. Scaling to massive models (e.g., Qwen-3) reveals a phase transition, achieving near-perfect accuracy (~100%) on standard tasks while maintaining 75% precision on specially constructed remote homology datasets. Chain-of-Thought interpretability reveals that these models transcend simple sequence alignment, leveraging implicit structural knowledge to perform reasoning akin to "mental folding." We formalize this cross-modal universality through the BioPAWS benchmark. Our work establishes a minimalist paradigm for AI for Science, proving that abstract logical structures distilled from human language constitute a powerful cognitive prior for decoding the complex syntax of biology.

papers.title: FaithfulSAE: Towards Capturing Faithful Features with Sparse Autoencoders without External Dataset Dependencies
papers.research_question: How does training Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) on out-of-distribution data affect their stability and feature faithfulness, and can training on the model's own synthetic data improve these aspects?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes FaithfulSAE, a method to train Sparse Autoencoders on the model's own synthetic data, which improves feature stability and reduces fake features compared to training on external datasets.
papers.conclusion: Training SAEs on the model's own synthetic data (FaithfulSAE) improves feature consistency and reduces fake features, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features.
papers.key_findings:
FaithfulSAEs trained on synthetic data show higher stability across seeds compared to SAEs trained on instruction datasets.
FaithfulSAEs achieve lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models compared to web-based dataset trained SAEs.
FaithfulSAEs outperform web-based SAEs in SAE probing tasks, indicating better reconstruction of the model's hidden state.
Shared Feature Ratio is higher when the target model and source model for synthetic data are the same, indicating that SAE training on its own data is more stable.
papers.limitation:
Lack of evaluation on instruction-tuned or reasoning models.
Shared Feature Ratio may not fully reflect the complexity of high-dimensional feature spaces.
Did not assess the interpretability of individual features through case studies.
future_direction: Exploring improved dataset generation and training strategies that could completely outperform Web-based methods.
Evaluating whether Faithful SAEs provide meaningful and interpretable explanations for individual features through detailed case studies.
Investigating the connection between pruning Fake Features and the principle of Minimal Description Length.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising solution for decomposing large language model representations into interpretable features. However, Paulo and Belrose (2025) have highlighted instability across different initialization seeds, and Heap et al. (2025) have pointed out that SAEs may not capture model-internal features. These problems likely stem from training SAEs on external datasets - either collected from the Web or generated by another model - which may contain out-of-distribution (OOD) data beyond the model's generalisation capabilities. This can result in hallucinated SAE features, which we term "Fake Features", that misrepresent the model's internal activations. To address these issues, we propose FaithfulSAE, a method that trains SAEs on the model's own synthetic dataset. Using FaithfulSAEs, we demonstrate that training SAEs on less-OOD instruction datasets results in SAEs being more stable across seeds. Notably, FaithfulSAEs outperform SAEs trained on web-based datasets in the SAE probing task and exhibit a lower Fake Feature Ratio in 5 out of 7 models. Overall, our approach eliminates the dependency on external datasets, advancing interpretability by better capturing model-internal features while highlighting the often neglected importance of SAE training datasets.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: DB-KSVD: Scalable Alternating Optimization for Disentangling High-Dimensional Embedding Spaces
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether sparse autoencoders (SAEs) find strong solutions to the dictionary learning problem for disentangling transformer embeddings, or if more sophisticated optimization approaches like the proposed DB-KSVD can achieve better performance.
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces DB-KSVD, a scalable dictionary learning algorithm for disentangling transformer embeddings, and shows it achieves competitive performance with sparse autoencoders on standard benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: The paper shows that alternating optimization algorithms can be scaled to problem sizes relevant for mechanistic interpretability of large transformer models, achieving competitive results with state-of-the-art SAE approaches on standardized metrics.
papers.key_findings:
DB-KSVD scales to millions of samples and thousands of dimensions, making it applicable to large transformer models.
DB-KSVD achieves competitive results with SAE-based approaches on the SAEBench metrics, suggesting both methods may be near theoretical limits.
Matryoshka structuring improves autointerpretability and absorption but slightly degrades loss recovered and spurious correlation removal.
DB-KSVD dictionaries tend to be coherent, especially for small sparsity, and Matryoshka structuring reduces coherence.
Initializing the dictionary with a partially known structure can significantly speed up convergence.
papers.limitation:
DB-KSVD is algorithmically more complex than SAE approaches, which makes implementation more challenging.
It is not clear whether the sample size used is sufficient or whether more scaling is needed to solve the disentanglement problem.
future_direction: Further investigation into using known structures to improve performance.
Exploring whether more scaling in sample size is needed for better disentanglement.
papers.abstract: Dictionary learning has recently emerged as a promising approach for mechanistic interpretability of large transformer models. Disentangling high-dimensional transformer embeddings, however, requires algorithms that scale to high-dimensional data with large sample sizes. Recent work has explored sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for this problem. However, SAEs use a simple linear encoder to solve the sparse encoding subproblem, which is known to be NP-hard. It is therefore interesting to understand whether this structure is sufficient to find good solutions to the dictionary learning problem or if a more sophisticated algorithm could find better solutions. In this work, we propose Double-Batch KSVD (DB-KSVD), a scalable dictionary learning algorithm that adapts the classic KSVD algorithm. DB-KSVD is informed by the rich theoretical foundations of KSVD but scales to datasets with millions of samples and thousands of dimensions. We demonstrate the efficacy of DB-KSVD by disentangling embeddings of the Gemma-2-2B model and evaluating on six metrics from the SAEBench benchmark, where we achieve competitive results when compared to established approaches based on SAEs. By matching SAE performance with an entirely different optimization approach, our results suggest that (i) SAEs do find strong solutions to the dictionary learning problem and (ii) that traditional optimization approaches can be scaled to the required problem sizes, offering a promising avenue for further research. We provide an implementation of DB-KSVD at https://github.com/RomeoV/KSVD.jl.

papers.title: SAEs $\textit{Can}$ Improve Unlearning: Dynamic Sparse Autoencoder Guardrails for Precision Unlearning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) be used to significantly improve machine unlearning in LLMs when employed dynamically, addressing the limitations of gradient-based methods?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG), a novel activation-based unlearning method that uses principled SAE feature selection and a dynamic classifier to achieve precise, efficient, and interpretable knowledge removal, outperforming gradient-based methods.
papers.conclusion: Dynamic SAE Guardrails (DSG) is an effective, efficient, and interpretable method for machine unlearning that addresses key limitations of gradient-based approaches and demonstrates that SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when used dynamically.
papers.key_findings:
DSG achieves a superior balance between forgetting target knowledge and preserving general utility compared to leading gradient-based and static SAE unlearning methods.
DSG offers greater computational efficiency and hyperparameter stability than gradient-based methods, requiring only forward passes and showing robust performance.
DSG demonstrates strong sequential unlearning capability, scalability to larger forget sets, and enhanced resistance to relearning attacks.
DSG is highly data-efficient and can perform zero-shot unlearning by leveraging semantically relevant SAE features identified without task-specific data.
DSG provides interpretable unlearning by targeting specific, semantically coherent SAE features associated with the knowledge to be removed.
papers.abstract: Machine unlearning is a promising approach to improve LLM safety by removing unwanted knowledge from the model. However, prevailing gradient-based unlearning methods suffer from issues such as high computational costs, hyperparameter instability, poor sequential unlearning capability, vulnerability to relearning attacks, low data efficiency, and lack of interpretability. While Sparse Autoencoders are well-suited to improve these aspects by enabling targeted activation-based unlearning, prior approaches underperform gradient-based methods. This work demonstrates that, contrary to these earlier findings, SAEs can significantly improve unlearning when employed dynamically. We introduce $\textbf{Dynamic DAE Guardrails}$ (DSG), a novel method for precision unlearning that leverages principled feature selection and a dynamic classifier. Our experiments show DSG substantially outperforms leading unlearning methods, achieving superior forget-utility trade-offs. DSG addresses key drawbacks of gradient-based approaches for unlearning -- offering enhanced computational efficiency and stability, robust performance in sequential unlearning, stronger resistance to relearning attacks, better data efficiency including zero-shot settings, and more interpretable unlearning.

papers.title: Towards Principled Evaluations of Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability and Control
papers.research_question: How to evaluate sparse autoencoders for interpretability and control in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against supervised feature dictionaries.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for evaluating sparse autoencoders using supervised feature dictionaries as a benchmark, applied to the IOI task.
papers.conclusion: The framework provides a step towards more objective evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task but are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model.
Feature occlusion and feature over-splitting phenomena are observed in SAE training.
papers.limitation: The F1 score does not take into account the magnitude of feature activations and is a conservative metric.
future_direction: Address limitations of the F1 score in interpretability evaluations
papers.abstract: Disentangling model activations into meaningful features is a central problem in interpretability. However, the absence of ground-truth for these features in realistic scenarios makes validating recent approaches, such as sparse dictionary learning, elusive. To address this challenge, we propose a framework for evaluating feature dictionaries in the context of specific tasks, by comparing them against \emph{supervised} feature dictionaries. First, we demonstrate that supervised dictionaries achieve excellent approximation, control, and interpretability of model computations on the task. Second, we use the supervised dictionaries to develop and contextualize evaluations of unsupervised dictionaries along the same three axes. We apply this framework to the indirect object identification (IOI) task using GPT-2 Small, with sparse autoencoders (SAEs) trained on either the IOI or OpenWebText datasets. We find that these SAEs capture interpretable features for the IOI task, but they are less successful than supervised features in controlling the model. Finally, we observe two qualitative phenomena in SAE training: feature occlusion (where a causally relevant concept is robustly overshadowed by even slightly higher-magnitude ones in the learned features), and feature over-splitting (where binary features split into many smaller, less interpretable features). We hope that our framework will provide a useful step towards more objective and grounded evaluations of sparse dictionary learning methods.

papers.title: On the transferability of Sparse Autoencoders for interpreting compressed models
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) trained on uncompressed models be effectively transferred to interpret compressed (pruned) models, and is pruning the original SAE itself a viable alternative to training a new SAE on the pruned model?
papers.core_contribution: SAEs pretrained on uncompressed models can be transferred to pruned models with minimal performance loss, and pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, offering a computationally efficient alternative.
papers.conclusion: Retraining SAEs for each compressed model variant may be unnecessary; pruning the pretrained SAE offers a practical and computationally efficient alternative for post-hoc interpretability analysis of compressed models.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model with only slight performance degradation compared to SAEs trained on the compressed model.
Pruning a pretrained SAE (e.g., to 25% sparsity) yields performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model, eliminating the need for costly retraining.
The transferability and pruning effectiveness hold across different model architectures (GPT-2 and Gemma-2-2B) and across various interpretability metrics (reconstruction, feature absorption, SCR, TPP, RAVEL).
future_direction: Explore the generalization of these findings to quantized and low-rank compressed models.
Further investigate the role of pruning as an implicit regularizer in interpretability systems.
papers.abstract: Modern LLMs face inference efficiency challenges due to their scale. To address this, many compression methods have been proposed, such as pruning and quantization. However, the effect of compression on a model's interpretability remains elusive. While several model interpretation approaches exist, such as circuit discovery, Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have proven particularly effective in decomposing a model's activation space into its feature basis. In this work, we explore the differences in SAEs for the original and compressed models. We find that SAEs trained on the original model can interpret the compressed model albeit with slight performance degradation compared to the trained SAE on the compressed model. Furthermore, simply pruning the original SAE itself achieves performance comparable to training a new SAE on the pruned model. This finding enables us to mitigate the extensive training costs of SAEs.

papers.title: Which Sparse Autoencoder Features Are Real? Model-X Knockoffs for False Discovery Rate Control
papers.research_question: How can we distinguish real computational patterns from erroneous correlations in sparse autoencoder features? The paper investigates using Model-X knockoffs for false discovery rate control in SAE feature selection.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Model-X knockoffs for selecting sparse autoencoder features with false discovery rate control, revealing that only 25% of highly active SAE features encode genuine task-relevant information.
papers.conclusion: The method provides a rigorous statistical framework for identifying genuine SAE features with FDR control, addressing a critical gap in interpretability research and showing that naive feature analysis approaches are dominated by false positives.
papers.key_findings:
The method selected 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 from 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification.
Selected features show a 5.40× separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features.
Only about 25% of the examined latents carry task-relevant signal, while 75% do not.
A classifier using only the selected features achieved 77.4% training accuracy.
Features with negative knockoff statistics exist, indicating misleading patterns that would be selected by naive correlation-based approaches.
papers.limitation:
Feature reduction is necessary for stable covariance estimation (n > p), which may miss rare but important features.
Computational cost scales quadratically in p, becoming expensive for very large feature sets.
The method identifies which features are real but does not explain what those features represent.
The method identifies statistical association, not necessarily causal importance.
future_direction: Explore hierarchical testing strategies, approximate knockoff methods, or alternative covariance estimation techniques to handle p ≫ n settings.
Combine knockoff-based selection with automated interpretation pipelines to provide both statistical validation and conceptual understanding.
Investigate how feature validity varies across layers and tasks, and how selection interacts with different SAE training objectives and architectures.
papers.abstract: Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are crucial for identifying interpretable features in neural networks, it is still challenging to distinguish between real computational patterns and erroneous correlations. We introduce Model-X knockoffs to SAE feature selection, using knock-off+ to control the false discovery rate (FDR) with finite-sample guarantees under the standard Model-X assumptions (in our case, via a Gaussian surrogate for the latent distribution). We select 129 features at a target FDR q=0.1 after analyzing 512 high-activity SAE latents for sentiment classification using Pythia-70M. About 25% of the latents under examination carry task-relevant signal, whereas 75% do not, according to the chosen set, which displays a 5.40x separation in knockoff statistics compared to non-selected features. Our method offers a re-producible and principled framework for reliable feature discovery by combining SAEs with multiple-testing-aware inference, advancing the foundations of mechanistic interpretability.

papers.title: Incorporating Hierarchical Semantics in Sparse Autoencoder Architectures
papers.research_question: Does incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improve the reconstruction-interpretability frontier? Specifically, does it improve reconstruction, maintain or improve interpretability, and learn hierarchical semantics?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (H-SAE) architecture that explicitly models semantic hierarchy, improving reconstruction performance and interpretability while being computationally efficient.
papers.conclusion: Incorporating hierarchical structure into sparse autoencoder architectures improves the reconstruction-interpretability frontier, leading to better reconstruction, maintained or improved interpretability, and learned hierarchical semantics.
papers.key_findings:
H-SAEs have better reconstruction performance than standard SAEs as measured by explained variance and downstream CE loss.
H-SAEs maintain or improve interpretability, showing less feature absorption and fewer redundant features across languages.
The H-SAE architecture learns hierarchical semantics, with high-level features capturing general concepts and low-level features capturing specific instances.
The hierarchical structure provides significant computational efficiency gains, allowing scaling to larger effective dictionary sizes with minimal overhead.
The architecture successfully translates theoretical insights about hierarchical concept geometry into a practical mixture-of-experts type model.
papers.limitation: Results are still imperfect, with some hard-to-interpret features and far from perfect reconstruction.
future_direction: Explore other reconstruction objectives beyond Euclidean distance.
Incorporate insights from causal representation learning into LLM interpretability.
papers.abstract: Sparse dictionary learning (and, in particular, sparse autoencoders) attempts to learn a set of human-understandable concepts that can explain variation on an abstract space. A basic limitation of this approach is that it neither exploits nor represents the semantic relationships between the learned concepts. In this paper, we introduce a modified SAE architecture that explicitly models a semantic hierarchy of concepts. Application of this architecture to the internal representations of large language models shows both that semantic hierarchy can be learned, and that doing so improves both reconstruction and interpretability. Additionally, the architecture leads to significant improvements in computational efficiency.

papers.title: BERTology Meets Biology: Interpreting Attention in Protein Language Models
papers.research_question: What does attention in protein Transformer language models capture about protein structure and function?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that attention in protein language models captures high-level structural and functional properties of proteins, and that attention focuses on progressively more complex properties with increasing layer depth.
papers.conclusion: Attention in protein Transformer models recovers structural and functional properties of proteins, and interpretability methods can aid scientific discovery.
papers.key_findings:
Attention in deep layers aligns with contact maps, connecting amino acids that are spatially close in 3D structure but far in sequence.
Attention targets binding sites and post-translational modifications, key functional components.
Attention heads specialize in particular amino acids and their patterns are consistent with substitution matrices.
Deeper layers focus more on high-level properties (binding sites, contacts) while secondary structure is targeted more evenly across layers.
Knowledge in embeddings accumulates gradually over layers, while attention acquires knowledge primarily in final layers.
papers.limitation: The analyses are associative and do not establish causal links between attention and model behavior.
future_direction: Using attention and learned representations as tools for scientific discovery.
Developing contextual visualizations of learned representations for domain experts in scientific domains.
papers.abstract: Abstract Transformer architectures have proven to learn useful representations for protein classification and generation tasks. However, these representations present challenges in interpretability. Through the lens of attention, we analyze the inner workings of the Transformer and explore how the model discerns structural and functional properties of proteins. We show that attention (1) captures the folding structure of proteins, connecting amino acids that are far apart in the underlying sequence, but spatially close in the three-dimensional structure, (2) targets binding sites, a key functional component of proteins, and (3) focuses on progressively more complex biophysical properties with increasing layer depth. We also present a three-dimensional visualization of the interaction between attention and protein structure. Our findings align with known biological processes and provide a tool to aid discovery in protein engineering and synthetic biology. The code for visualization and analysis is available at https://github.com/salesforce/provis .

papers.title: Insights into a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model with sparse autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders be applied to interpret the internal representations of a radiology-specialised multimodal large language model (MAIRA-2) and steer its generations?
papers.core_contribution: This work applies Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology MLLM MAIRA-2, identifying a subset of interpretable clinical concepts within its representations and demonstrating the feasibility and challenges of steering model generations using these features.
papers.conclusion: The study provides initial insights into the internal concepts of MAIRA-2 using SAEs, marking a step toward mechanistic interpretability, while highlighting practical and methodological challenges in automated interpretability and steering.
papers.key_findings:
A small subset (1.8%) of SAE features are highly interpretable (F1 > 0.75), corresponding to clinically relevant concepts like medical devices, pathologies, and textual features.
Nearly half (46%) of SAE features are not interpretable by the automated pipeline (F1 < 0.5).
Steering model generations using SAE features is possible but produces more off-target changes than on-target changes, with success highly dependent on the specific feature.
There is a strong correlation between the on-target effects of positive and negative steering coefficients.
The trained SAEs and their automated interpretations are publicly released to foster further research.
papers.limitation:
Many SAE features (46%) are not interpretable by the automated pipeline.
Steering often produces more off-target changes than on-target changes.
The study reveals practical and methodological challenges across the SAE training, automated concept discovery, and steering pipeline.
papers.abstract: Interpretability can improve the safety, transparency and trust of AI models, which is especially important in healthcare applications where decisions often carry significant consequences. Mechanistic interpretability, particularly through the use of sparse autoencoders (SAEs), offers a promising approach for uncovering human-interpretable features within large transformer-based models. In this study, we apply Matryoshka-SAE to the radiology-specialised multimodal large language model, MAIRA-2, to interpret its internal representations. Using large-scale automated interpretability of the SAE features, we identify a range of clinically relevant concepts - including medical devices (e.g., line and tube placements, pacemaker presence), pathologies such as pleural effusion and cardiomegaly, longitudinal changes and textual features. We further examine the influence of these features on model behaviour through steering, demonstrating directional control over generations with mixed success. Our results reveal practical and methodological challenges, yet they offer initial insights into the internal concepts learned by MAIRA-2 - marking a step toward deeper mechanistic understanding and interpretability of a radiology-adapted multimodal large language model, and paving the way for improved model transparency. We release the trained SAEs and interpretations: https://huggingface.co/microsoft/maira-2-sae.

papers.title: Analyze Feature Flow to Enhance Interpretation and Steering in Language Models
papers.research_question: How do features discovered by sparse autoencoders evolve across consecutive layers of large language models, and how can this understanding be used for interpretability and model steering?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a data-free cosine similarity method to map Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features across transformer layers, creating flow graphs that reveal feature evolution and enable precise model steering through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.conclusion: The proposed cross-layer feature mapping framework provides granular interpretability of feature evolution in LLMs and offers a new, transparent method for steering model behavior through targeted feature manipulation.
papers.key_findings:
Cosine similarity between SAE decoder weights effectively identifies feature relationships across layers, validated against activation correlations.
Feature formation follows distinct patterns: early layers show high entropy and feature birth, middle layers stabilize, and later layers primarily propagate existing features.
Deactivating predecessor features identified by the top-1 cosine match is causally effective, outperforming random selection.
Multi-layer steering using flow graphs is more effective and less sensitive to hyperparameters than single-layer interventions.
Flow graphs provide mechanistic insights, revealing how semantic meaning (e.g., 'particle physics') evolves and transforms across the model's computational pathway.
papers.limitation: The current steering procedure operates locally on hidden states and may not fully redirect the model's computational trajectory to a different 'minima' for truly efficient deactivation or activation.
future_direction: Further research on flow graphs as a unit of study for model interpretability.
Extending the steering experiments and flow graph analysis to other model architectures like Llama Scope.
Investigating the method's applicability and performance across a wider range of models and SAE training configurations.
papers.abstract: We introduce a new approach to systematically map features discovered by sparse autoencoder across consecutive layers of large language models, extending earlier work that examined inter-layer feature links. By using a data-free cosine similarity technique, we trace how specific features persist, transform, or first appear at each stage. This method yields granular flow graphs of feature evolution, enabling fine-grained interpretability and mechanistic insights into model computations. Crucially, we demonstrate how these cross-layer feature maps facilitate direct steering of model behavior by amplifying or suppressing chosen features, achieving targeted thematic control in text generation. Together, our findings highlight the utility of a causal, cross-layer interpretability framework that not only clarifies how features develop through forward passes but also provides new means for transparent manipulation of large language models.

papers.title: Analysis of Variational Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: We investigate whether incorporating variational methods into SAE architectures can improve feature organization and interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Variational Sparse Autoencoder (vSAE) and finds that it underperforms standard SAEs due to excessive KL divergence regularization causing feature death, disproving the hypothesis that variational methods improve feature organization.
papers.conclusion: The naive application of variational methods to sparse autoencoders does not improve feature organization or interpretability and is not a promising direction for SAE development.
papers.key_findings:
The vSAE underperforms the standard TopK SAE across core metrics like CE loss, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
The vSAE exhibits catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to KL divergence pressure pushing activations toward zero.
The vSAE shows improved performance on Spurious Correlation Removal (SCR) and Targeted Probe Perturbation (TPP) benchmarks, indicating more independent features.
t-SNE visualizations reveal that vSAE features are more dispersed and less clustered than SAE features, supporting the dispersive pressure hypothesis.
Despite having far fewer active features, the vSAE maintains feature interpretability, but the overall performance degradation suggests variational methods are not beneficial for SAEs.
papers.limitation:
The vSAE suffers from catastrophic feature death, with 82% fewer living features than the standard SAE, due to excessive KL divergence regularization.
The observed improvements in feature independence (SCR, TPP) may be an artifact of the reduced dictionary size rather than principled organization.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach for interpreting neural network representations by learning sparse, human-interpretable features from dense activations. We investigate whether incorporating variational methods into SAE architectures can improve feature organization and interpretability. We introduce the Variational Sparse Autoencoder (vSAE), which replaces deterministic ReLU gating with stochastic sampling from learned Gaussian posteriors and incorporates KL divergence regularization toward a standard normal prior. Our hypothesis is that this probabilistic sampling creates dispersive pressure, causing features to organize more coherently in the latent space while avoiding overlap. We evaluate a TopK vSAE against a standard TopK SAE on Pythia-70M transformer residual stream activations using comprehensive benchmarks including SAE Bench, individual feature interpretability analysis, and global latent space visualization through t-SNE. The vSAE underperforms standard SAE across core evaluation metrics, though excels at feature independence and ablation metrics. The KL divergence term creates excessive regularization pressure that substantially reduces the fraction of living features, leading to observed performance degradation. While vSAE features demonstrate improved robustness, they exhibit many more dead features than baseline. Our findings suggest that naive application of variational methods to SAEs does not improve feature organization or interpretability.

papers.title: Improving Steering Vectors by Targeting Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we improve steering vectors to target specific SAE features and achieve desired model behaviors while minimizing unintended side effects?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a method to measure steering effects using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) and uses this to develop SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which constructs steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects.
papers.conclusion: SAE-TS is an effective method for steering language models, balancing desired behavioral changes with output coherence better than existing baselines.
papers.key_findings:
Developed a method to quantify and interpret the effects of steering interventions on SAE features.
Introduced SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which learns a linear relationship between steering vectors and their effects on SAE features to construct targeted steering vectors.
SAE-TS outperforms existing methods like Contrastive Activation Addition (CAA) and direct SAE feature steering on most tasks, achieving better alignment with intended behavior while maintaining coherence.
The method allows for more predictable and controllable steering of language models compared to prior approaches.
Provides an interactive tool (EffectVis) for exploring feature effects and relationships.
papers.limitation:
Investigations were limited to Gemma-2 2B and 9B models, which share the same distilled architecture, so results may not transfer to other models.
Focused on base models without instruction tuning, so the study did not investigate tasks and features relevant for safety or capabilities.
Steering is limited to concepts present in the SAE, which may not cover all concepts due to feature splitting or niche features only appearing in very large SAEs.
future_direction: Apply steering methods to chat models and safety-relevant steering targets.
Explore different SAE architectures (e.g., TopK SAEs) and test on various model architectures beyond the Gemma family.
Adapt BiPO to optimize steering vectors towards desired feature effects.
papers.abstract: To control the behavior of language models, steering methods attempt to ensure that outputs of the model satisfy specific pre-defined properties. Adding steering vectors to the model is a promising method of model control that is easier than finetuning, and may be more robust than prompting. However, it can be difficult to anticipate the effects of steering vectors produced by methods such as CAA [Panickssery et al., 2024] or the direct use of SAE latents [Templeton et al., 2024]. In our work, we address this issue by using SAEs to measure the effects of steering vectors, giving us a method that can be used to understand the causal effect of any steering vector intervention. We use this method for measuring causal effects to develop an improved steering method, SAE-Targeted Steering (SAE-TS), which finds steering vectors to target specific SAE features while minimizing unintended side effects. We show that overall, SAE-TS balances steering effects with coherence better than CAA and SAE feature steering, when evaluated on a range of tasks.

papers.title: AdaptiveK Sparse Autoencoders: Dynamic Sparsity Allocation for Interpretable LLM Representations
papers.research_question: How can we define semantic simplicity or complexity within LLM representation spaces, and how can this be used to dynamically adjust sparsity in sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces AdaptiveK SAE, a sparse autoencoder framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on input complexity, improving reconstruction and interpretability without extensive hyperparameter tuning.
papers.conclusion: AdaptiveK SAE provides an efficient and effective method for interpretable feature extraction in LLMs by dynamically allocating sparsity based on input complexity.
papers.key_findings:
Text complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, as demonstrated by linear probes.
Adaptive sparsity allocation based on complexity improves reconstruction quality and interpretability metrics across multiple model scales.
AdaptiveK SAE outperforms fixed-sparsity baselines on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, and cosine similarity.
papers.limitation: Due to cost constraints, the study used a smaller training dataset (250,000 contexts) compared to the 500,000,000 tokens used in SAEBench.
papers.abstract: Understanding the internal representations of large language models (LLMs) remains a central challenge for interpretability research. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) offer a promising solution by decomposing activations into interpretable features, but existing approaches rely on fixed sparsity constraints that fail to account for input complexity. We propose AdaptiveK SAE (Adaptive Top K Sparse Autoencoders), a novel framework that dynamically adjusts sparsity levels based on the semantic complexity of each input. Leveraging linear probes, we demonstrate that context complexity is linearly encoded in LLM representations, and we use this signal to guide feature allocation during training. Experiments across ten language models (from 70M to 14B parameters) demonstrate that this complexity-driven adaptation significantly outperforms fixed-sparsity approaches on reconstruction fidelity, explained variance, cosine similarity and interpretability metrics while eliminating the computational burden of extensive hyperparameter tuning.

papers.title: AlignSAE: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we align Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) features with human-defined concepts to create an interpretable and controllable interface for Large Language Models?
papers.core_contribution: ALIGNSAE is a method that aligns Sparse Autoencoder features with a predefined ontology through a two-stage training curriculum, enabling precise concept-level inspection and control in frozen LLMs.
papers.conclusion: ALIGNSAE provides a verifiable and controllable interface for concept-level manipulation in LLMs, advancing interpretability and steering capabilities.
papers.key_findings:
ALIGNSAE achieves near-perfect concept-slot binding in mid-layers (e.g., layer 6) of GPT-2, with diagonal accuracy up to 1.00.
It significantly reduces concept fragmentation and increases top-1 concentration compared to traditional unsupervised SAEs.
Swap interventions demonstrate reliable controllability with a clear fidelity-strength tradeoff, achieving up to 0.847 swap success at layer 6.
In 2-hop reasoning, ALIGNSAE attains 4× higher swap success than traditional SAE.
The method provides mechanistic insights into grokking-like generalization dynamics via step-wise concept binding.
papers.limitation:
The method is evaluated on a limited ontology (6 relations for 1-hop, 20 for 2-hop) and on GPT-2, a relatively small model, which may not reflect performance on larger models or more complex ontologies.
Swap controllability has a narrow effective amplification range (around α=2), and over-amplification can destabilize interventions.
future_direction: Extending ALIGNSAE to larger ontologies and more complex concept types.
Applying the method to larger language models and more diverse tasks.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) encode factual knowledge within hidden parametric spaces that are difficult to inspect or control. While Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can decompose hidden activations into more fine-grained, interpretable features, they often struggle to reliably align these features with human-defined concepts, resulting in entangled and distributed feature representations. To address this, we introduce AlignSAE, a method that aligns SAE features with a predefined ontology through a "pre-train, then post-train" curriculum. After an initial unsupervised training phase, we apply supervised post-training to bind specific concepts to dedicated latent slots while preserving the remaining capacity for general reconstruction. This separation creates an interpretable interface where specific concepts can be inspected and controlled without interference from unrelated features. Empirical results demonstrate that AlignSAE enables precise causal interventions, such as reliable "concept swaps", by targeting single, semantically aligned slots, and further supports multi-hop reasoning and a mechanistic probe of grokking-like generalization dynamics.

papers.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we train sparse autoencoders to learn hierarchical features and avoid pathologies like feature absorption and splitting when scaling dictionary size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders, a hierarchical variant that trains multiple nested dictionaries simultaneously to learn features at different levels of abstraction, reducing feature absorption and splitting.
papers.conclusion: Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical interpretability tasks, enabling training of arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Matryoshka SAEs significantly reduce feature absorption and splitting compared to standard SAEs.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve more disentangled latent representations and better performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks.
Matryoshka SAEs maintain or improve downstream task performance with increasing dictionary size, unlike standard SAEs which often degrade.
Matryoshka SAEs exhibit a small trade-off in reconstruction fidelity but learn more meaningful features that result in comparable downstream model loss.
The hierarchical structure forces early latents to capture general concepts and later latents to specialize, preserving interpretable features at multiple scales.
papers.limitation:
Slightly reduced reconstruction performance compared to standard SAEs.
Increased training time due to multiple nested reconstruction objectives.
Reliance on quantitative metrics that may not fully capture human-relevant interpretability.
future_direction: Investigate the human interpretability of Matryoshka SAE latents.
Explore the applicability of Matryoshka SAEs to practical interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting neural networks by extracting the concepts represented in their activations. However, choosing the size of the SAE dictionary (i.e. number of learned concepts) creates a tension: as dictionary size increases to capture more relevant concepts, sparsity incentivizes features to be split or absorbed into more specific features, leaving high-level features missing or warped. We introduce Matryoshka SAEs, a novel variant that addresses these issues by simultaneously training multiple nested dictionaries of increasing size, forcing the smaller dictionaries to independently reconstruct the inputs without using the larger dictionaries. This organizes features hierarchically - the smaller dictionaries learn general concepts, while the larger dictionaries learn more specific concepts, without incentive to absorb the high-level features. We train Matryoshka SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and TinyStories and find superior performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks, more disentangled concept representations, and reduced feature absorption. While there is a minor tradeoff with reconstruction performance, we believe Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical tasks, as they enable training arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoder Neural Operators: Model Recovery in Function Spaces
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be extended to operate in infinite-dimensional function spaces for concept learning, and what advantages do functional representations offer over standard SAEs?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces sparse autoencoder neural operators (SAE-NOs) that operate in function spaces, specifically SAE-FNOs, which improve concept learning stability, robustness, and generalization compared to standard SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Functional representations in SAE-NOs extend sparse autoencoders from detectors of concept presence to models that capture the underlying structure of the data, highlighting parameterization as a central driver of interpretability and generalization.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-FNO successfully recovers ground-truth concepts in synthetic data and converges to zero dictionary recovery error.
SAE-FNO generalizes to unseen input resolutions, unlike SAE-CNN which fails beyond training resolution.
SAE-FNO learns concepts that are stable across different sparsity levels and exhibit diverse correlations, overcoming the orthogonality bias of SAE-MLP.
SAE-FNO achieves higher concept utilization efficiency, requiring fewer concepts to represent data, especially for larger domains.
Lifting accelerates concept recovery by acting as a preconditioner and improves optimization.
papers.abstract: We frame the problem of unifying representations in neural models as one of sparse model recovery and introduce a framework that extends sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to lifted spaces and infinite-dimensional function spaces, enabling mechanistic interpretability of large neural operators (NO). While the Platonic Representation Hypothesis suggests that neural networks converge to similar representations across architectures, the representational properties of neural operators remain underexplored despite their growing importance in scientific computing. We compare the inference and training dynamics of SAEs, lifted-SAE, and SAE neural operators. We highlight how lifting and operator modules introduce beneficial inductive biases, enabling faster recovery, improved recovery of smooth concepts, and robust inference across varying resolutions, a property unique to neural operators.

papers.title: From Atoms to Trees: Building a Structured Feature Forest with Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to capture the hierarchical structure of features in LLM representations, moving beyond isolated feature extraction?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (HSAE), a method that jointly learns sparse autoencoders and parent-child relationships to extract hierarchical feature structures from LLM representations.
papers.conclusion: HSAE is a novel framework that learns conceptual hierarchies from LLM activations, outperforming post-hoc methods and preserving SAE feature quality.
papers.key_findings:
HSAE recovers semantically meaningful hierarchies from LLM activations, as shown by qualitative case studies and quantitative metrics.
HSAE significantly outperforms post-hoc alignment baselines in hierarchical consistency (e.g., lower Hamming distance, higher co-activation probabilities).
HSAE maintains feature quality and reconstruction fidelity comparable to standard SAEs across various dictionary sizes.
The learned hierarchies manifest geometrically: activations triggering sibling features cluster together in the activation space.
Features with multiple children exhibit higher interpretability (AutoInterp scores) than those with a single child.
papers.limitation:
The tree structure is constrained by a fixed number of levels, which may not fully capture varying depths of semantic abstraction.
Some misalignments in parent-child co-activation persist, and it is unclear if they are due to methodological constraints or inherently non-hierarchical activations.
future_direction: Investigate more flexible architectural priors and scaling laws of hierarchical discovery.
Apply hierarchies for multi-scale model steering and safety auditing.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have proven effective for extracting monosemantic features from large language models (LLMs), yet these features are typically identified in isolation. However, broad evidence suggests that LLMs capture the intrinsic structure of natural language, where the phenomenon of "feature splitting" in particular indicates that such structure is hierarchical. To capture this, we propose the Hierarchical Sparse Autoencoder (HSAE), which jointly learns a series of SAEs and the parent-child relationships between their features. HSAE strengthens the alignment between parent and child features through two novel mechanisms: a structural constraint loss and a random feature perturbation mechanism. Extensive experiments across various LLMs and layers demonstrate that HSAE consistently recovers semantically meaningful hierarchies, supported by both qualitative case studies and rigorous quantitative metrics. At the same time, HSAE preserves the reconstruction fidelity and interpretability of standard SAEs across different dictionary sizes. Our work provides a powerful, scalable tool for discovering and analyzing the multi-scale conceptual structures embedded in LLM representations.

papers.title: Improving Dictionary Learning with Gated Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can sparse autoencoders be improved to reduce biases like shrinkage and achieve better sparsity and reconstruction fidelity in language model activations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Gated SAEs that decouple feature detection and magnitude estimation, solving shrinkage and providing Pareto improvements in sparsity and reconstruction fidelity over baseline SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Gated SAEs are a promising improvement for sparse autoencoders in mechanistic interpretability, offering better performance and reduced biases.
papers.key_findings:
Gated SAEs achieve better reconstruction fidelity at any given level of sparsity compared to baseline SAEs.
Gated SAEs effectively address the shrinkage problem, with reconstructions being unbiased.
Gated SAE features are similarly interpretable to baseline SAE features based on human evaluation.
Ablation studies show that freezing the decoder in the auxiliary task and weight tying are important for performance.
papers.abstract: Recent work has found that sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are an effective technique for unsupervised discovery of interpretable features in language models' (LMs) activations, by finding sparse, linear reconstructions of LM activations. We introduce the Gated Sparse Autoencoder (Gated SAE), which achieves a Pareto improvement over training with prevailing methods. In SAEs, the L1 penalty used to encourage sparsity introduces many undesirable biases, such as shrinkage -- systematic underestimation of feature activations. The key insight of Gated SAEs is to separate the functionality of (a) determining which directions to use and (b) estimating the magnitudes of those directions: this enables us to apply the L1 penalty only to the former, limiting the scope of undesirable side effects. Through training SAEs on LMs of up to 7B parameters we find that, in typical hyper-parameter ranges, Gated SAEs solve shrinkage, are similarly interpretable, and require half as many firing features to achieve comparable reconstruction fidelity.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Generalize? A Case Study of Answerability
papers.research_question: Can sparse autoencoders capture abstract concepts like answerability in a way that generalizes across diverse datasets?
papers.core_contribution: SAE features for answerability show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, sometimes generalizing well and sometimes poorly, indicating the need for better evaluation methods for SAE-based interpretability.
papers.conclusion: Comprehensive out-of-distribution evaluation is critical for SAE-based interpretability, as SAE features show inconsistent generalization, highlighting the need for better evaluation methods.
papers.key_findings:
Residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains for answerability detection.
SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain generalization, with performance varying from near-random to better than residual stream probes.
Standard SAE feature search can fail to identify generalizing features even when they exist.
Linear probes on the residual stream also exhibit high variance in generalization across datasets.
Combining multiple SAE features does not improve out-of-domain performance over the best single feature.
papers.limitation:
Evaluation is limited to Gemma 2 due to lack of high-quality SAEs for other instruction-tuned LLMs.
SAE features depend on training hyperparameters and data, affecting generalizability.
Simple SAE probe training techniques were used, which may not yield optimal results.
Feature splitting in SAEs may cause abstract concepts like answerability to be split into many separate features, complicating detection.
future_direction: Developing better evaluation methods for SAE feature generalization.
Improving SAE training methods to encourage learning of general features.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising approach in language model interpretability, offering unsupervised extraction of sparse features. For interpretability methods to succeed, they must identify abstract features across domains, and these features can often manifest differently in each context. We examine this through "answerability" - a model's ability to recognize answerable questions. We extensively evaluate SAE feature generalization across diverse, partly self-constructed answerability datasets for Gemma 2 SAEs. Our analysis reveals that residual stream probes outperform SAE features within domains, but generalization performance differs sharply. SAE features show inconsistent out-of-domain transfer, with performance varying from almost random to outperforming residual stream probes. Overall, this demonstrates the need for robust evaluation methods and quantitative approaches to predict feature generalization in SAE-based interpretability.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of Sparse Autoencoder and Activation Difference in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve language model steering by selecting the most relevant sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and applying a token-wise decaying steering strategy to avoid degenerate outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method to select the most relevant SAE feature for steering and introduces a token-wise decaying steering strategy, which improves stability and performance in mathematical reasoning and instruction following tasks.
papers.conclusion: Decaying SAE steering is an effective method for controlling language model behavior, providing a more interpretable alternative to mean activation difference, especially in mathematical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE steering with a single relevant feature and decaying strategy outperforms constant steering and mean activation difference in math reasoning.
SAE steering can elicit step-by-step mathematical reasoning without few-shot prompts.
In instruction following, SAE steering matches the performance of mean activation difference.
The proposed feature selection method effectively removes redundant SAE features.
Decaying steering avoids degenerate outputs such as repetitive words.
papers.limitation:
The proposed method struggles with word inclusion tasks, as no single SAE feature reliably encodes lexical constraints.
The explanations from Neuronpedia are not guaranteed to be precise.
future_direction: Finer-grained SAE combinations for language proximity cases.
Multilingual-aware alignment strategies for steering.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for language model steering. Prior work has explored top-k SAE latents for steering, but we observe that many dimensions among the top-k latents capture non-semantic features such as punctuation rather than semantic attributes like instructions. To address this, we propose focusing on a single, most relevant SAE latent (top-1), eliminating redundant features. We further identify a limitation in constant SAE steering, which often produces degenerate outputs such as repetitive single words. To mitigate this, we introduce a token-wise decaying steering strategy, enabling more faithful comparisons with mean activation difference baselines. Empirically, we show that steering an SAE latent associated with reasoning reliably elicits step-by-step mathematical reasoning and enhances inference quality, functionally resembling the effect of appending a guiding token. Our results demonstrate that SAEs outperform mean activation difference methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and match their performance on IF-Eval.

papers.title: Sparse but Wrong: Incorrect L0 Leads to Incorrect Features in Sparse Autoencoders
